prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Somewhere

outputs.L1:
Somewhere in Kentucky, she went for kicks—  
spiked polka-dot, mint-julep, Grade 1 stakes,  
white-gloved clubhouse how-you-do-sees—  
until all the horses broke their legs.

And for all the horses, my ex joined  
the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front,  
and she crashed all the Bentleys,  
and it was I who bled  
in Derby countryside, where horses die  
in Japanese slaughterhouses,  
defrocked  
of rose blanket and blue ribbon.

And how very they went  
into that kind of darkness, knowing  
only “My Old Kentucky Home”  
was no longer a run for the roses,  
but besieged  
with cannibals and thieves.

And only Millionaires’ Row sings:  
a hero is a horse without a heart  
that never aches  
for lovers who cross them  
one too many times.

When we kill one horse, all of them die,  
waiting  
long after Kentucky.

And she slips white gloves on my hands,  
bent from carrying her  
on NYC streets jammed the wrong way  
in every direction.

How merry are we—  
how merry,  
how bright-shine beaming,  
no longer weeping.

And she bears my head to the heat,  
and I let it all go,  
and bet my last hat and home.

And how—  
how very are we—  
and it changes everything.
outputs.L2:
In Kentucky, she chased amusement through Grade 1 stakes,  
through mint juleps, polka dots, spikes,  
white gloves and clubhouse greetings,  
until every horse shattered its legs.

For those horses, my former love enlisted  
in the Seine-et-Oise Thoroughbred Liberation Front,  
wrecked every Bentley,  
and I was the one left bleeding  
out in Derby country,  
where horses end up dying in Japanese slaughterhouses,  
stripped of rose garlands and blue ribbons.

How far they went,  
into a darkness that knew only this:  
my old Kentucky home was no longer  
a race for roses.  
It was under siege  
by cannibals and thieves.

Only Millionaires Row kept singing  
that a hero is a heartless horse,  
one that never suffers  
for lovers who betray it too many times.

When a single horse is killed,  
all horses perish with it,  
still waiting  
long after Kentucky is gone.

And she slides white gloves over my hands,  
hands crooked from carrying her  
through New York City streets  
clogged against every proper direction.

How joyful we are.  
How joyful.  
How radiant, shining,  
no longer crying.

She lifts my head toward the heat.  
I release everything.  
I wager my final hat and my home.

How—  
how deeply we are.

And it alters everything.
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents Kentucky horse racing as a world of glamour and tradition, but also as one built on violence. At first, the setting may appear celebratory: horse racing is associated with wealth, prestige, beautiful animals, famous events, and a long cultural history. However, the poem exposes the suffering beneath that polished surface. The excitement of the race depends on the bodies of horses pushed to their limits, and celebration is shadowed by injury, exploitation, and death.

The poem also suggests that the fate of one racehorse is not isolated. When an individual horse is harmed or destroyed, it represents a larger system of exploitation. The suffering of a single animal becomes symbolic of the suffering of all horses used for entertainment, profit, and status. In this way, the poem moves beyond one tragic event and criticizes the broader culture that turns living beings into disposable objects.

At the same time, the speaker’s personal life is woven into this violent world. Their relationship with an ex is marked by rebellion, damage, and emotional pain. The connection between them seems intense but destructive, shaped by acts of defiance and a shared closeness to danger. As the speaker reflects on the ex, the imagery of racing, injury, and sacrifice becomes tied to heartbreak. Personal grief and public violence mirror each other, making the relationship feel as wounded as the horses the poem describes.

Throughout the poem, images of wealth, tradition, and prestige are sharply contrasted with disturbing images of cannibalism, theft, slaughterhouses, and loss. This contrast reveals the hypocrisy behind the elegant surface of horse racing culture. What appears noble or refined is shown to depend on brutality. The poem forces the reader to see that luxury and violence are not separate in this world; instead, they exist together, with beauty often masking cruelty.

By the end, the speaker seems to surrender everything. This surrender suggests that love, grief, and sacrifice have deeply changed them. They are no longer simply observing the suffering around them; they have been transformed by it. The ending implies a loss of innocence and a recognition that love can demand painful forms of giving up. In the speaker’s final surrender, the poem brings together its central concerns: the cost of devotion, the violence hidden beneath beauty, and the way suffering can alter a person completely.
outputs.L4:
The poem confronts the violence, exploitation, and romanticized spectacle of horse racing through a surreal, fragmented elegy that blends Kentucky Derby imagery, personal heartbreak, and political revolt. Rather than treating the racetrack as a place of glamour, tradition, or harmless entertainment, the poem exposes it as a stage on which suffering is disguised as beauty. The horse’s body becomes the center of the poem’s moral vision: raced, watched, wagered on, and mourned only after it has been used up. Through images of speed, spectacle, wealth, blood, flowers, and public excitement, the poem reveals how easily cruelty can be aestheticized when it is surrounded by ceremony.

At the same time, the poem refuses to separate the death of the horse from other forms of loss and violence. Personal grief enters the poem alongside public outrage, so that heartbreak and political anger become inseparable. The speaker’s sorrow is not private or contained; it spills outward, implicating lovers, spectators, owners, bettors, and the social systems that turn living beings into instruments of pleasure and profit. The poem’s fragmented structure mirrors this emotional and ethical rupture. Its surreal shifts and broken associations suggest a world in which ordinary language is no longer adequate to describe the scale of harm.

By connecting the Kentucky Derby to broader histories of wealth, domination, and spectacle, the poem transforms an individual death into an accusation against an entire culture. The dead horse is not merely a symbol, but a presence whose suffering forces the speaker to see more clearly. In mourning the animal, the poem also mourns the damaged forms of love and community that allow such violence to continue. Yet the grief it expresses is not passive. It becomes a force of recognition, a demand for revolt, and a refusal to let beauty excuse brutality. Ultimately, the poem finds that the death of one horse implicates an entire world of lovers, wealth, and cruelty, making grief both collective and transformative.
outputs.L5:
**Somewhere**

Somewhere, beyond the noise of everyday life, there is a place where everything feels a little softer. It may not be marked on any map, and it may not have a name, but we know it exists. Somewhere is the place we imagine when we need hope, comfort, or a fresh start.

For some people, somewhere is a quiet beach at sunrise, where the waves move gently and the air smells of salt. For others, it is a small room filled with books, a mountain path, a busy city street, or the warmth of home after a long journey. Somewhere can be a destination, a memory, or even a dream waiting to become real.

The beauty of “somewhere” is that it belongs to everyone. It reminds us that life is not limited to where we are now. There is always another road, another chance, another place where things may be different. Somewhere, someone is beginning again. Somewhere, a door is opening. Somewhere, a dream is taking shape.

And perhaps the most important thing about somewhere is this: we do not always have to find it far away. Sometimes, somewhere is closer than we think. It can be found in a moment of peace, in a kind word, in a new idea, or in the courage to take one small step forward. Somewhere is not just a place—it is a possibility.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose poem about the Kentucky Derby, horse racing cruelty, wealth, heartbreak, and an ex-lover, using fragmented syntax, surreal imagery, ampersands, and no conventional line breaks.
counterfactuals.output: At the Derby the hats bloom like expensive wounds & the roses are red because money asked them nicely & because blood knows how to behave in public. You said you loved me beside the rail, or maybe beside a television, or maybe inside a glass of bourbon where the ice kept drowning its small transparent horses. The crowd leaned forward, all teeth & binoculars, praying for a body to become profit. Silk on the jockeys, foam on the mouths, thunder stitched into the track. Beneath the anthem, the animal question: how fast can heartbreak run before it breaks itself? I remember your hand leaving mine like a gate opening. I remember the rich clapping in weatherproof joy. I remember a filly with moonlight in her ankles, asked to be lightning until lightning became fracture. The dirt rose up, obedient & brown, covering everything—hoof, ticket, kiss, the ambulance with its soft mechanical hymn. Millionaires drank mint from silver cups while the horses carried their little apocalypses in public. You wore white. I wore the future badly. Somewhere a trainer whispered numbers into a trembling neck, somewhere a veterinarian folded mercy into a syringe, somewhere my heart placed another losing bet on return. & still they ran. Because the whip is an old language. Because beauty is often forced to perform for balconies. Because we call it tradition when the cruelty has a good tailor. Your laughter moved through the grandstand like a torn program. I wanted to forgive you, but the track kept circling, kept circling, an oval bruise with no exit. The winner disappeared beneath a blanket of roses, as if flowers could apologize. The losers limped back into the invisible. The dead became rumor before sunset. & I, wearing my ruined little crown of wanting, stood among the emptied cups & crushed tickets, listening to the wealth wash its hands, listening for your voice in the bugle’s gold throat, hearing only the start again, again, again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense, avant-garde poem in a contemporary American style that blends “My Old Kentucky Home,” Millionaires’ Row, rose blankets, racehorses, slaughterhouses, and a failed relationship in New York City.
counterfactuals.output:
**DOWN THE BACKSTRETCH, BROOKLYN**

In the vestibule of your walk-up  
I heard “My Old Kentucky Home” leak  
from a cracked phone speaker—  
not song, but weather,  
not weather, but debt  
wearing a white linen suit  
on Millionaires’ Row.

Everyone was crying into juleps.  
Everyone was beautiful as money  
pretending it had never been touched.  
The horses entered wearing thunder,  
ankles taped with prayer,  
names like litigation,  
like mother’s maiden name,  
like the thing we never said  
in the cab on Houston.

A rose blanket over the winner:  
red mouths sewn into one soft wound.  
A thousand petals applauding  
the animal for outrunning  
the arithmetic of its body.  
Behind the grandstand,  
behind the brass and bourbon,  
behind the television’s clean blue eye,  
the slaughterhouse practiced  
its hymn of hooks.

You loved New York  
because it never asked the horse  
if it wanted to be symbolic.  
I loved you because you could look  
at a skyline and call it hunger  
without apologizing.  
Our apartment filled with receipts,  
mint stems, black dresses,  
the sour chemistry of rain  
on trash night.  
We slept back-to-back  
like two countries  
sharing a poisoned river.

Down in Kentucky,  
the track glowed green  
as a rich man’s afterlife.  
The mares in the paddock  
rolled their eyes toward God  
or the cameras—  
who can tell the difference  
when both want spectacle?

I kept thinking: home  
is a song someone else profits from.  
Home is a mansion row  
of locked verandas.  
Home is your hand  
withdrawing from mine  
as the train hit DeKalb,  
as if tenderness were a wager  
you suddenly understood.

The bell rang.  
The gates opened.  
Everything living  
became velocity,  
became foam,  
became numbers climbing  
a screen in the bar  
where we did not speak.

By midnight the roses browned  
in hotel sinks.  
The horses dreamed in stalls  
of grass without fences.  
Somewhere a blade was rinsed  
and lifted again  
into the fluorescent mercy  
of work.

And you—  
you were already uptown,  
or gone,  
or becoming one more bright hat  
among the balconies,  
one more hand raised  
not to wave  
but to bet against me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a chaotic lyrical monologue about someone whose ex joins a fictional thoroughbred liberation front after a disastrous trip to Kentucky, with themes of animal suffering, class violence, and romantic ruin.
counterfactuals.output:
She came back from Kentucky with bluegrass in her cuffs and a look in her eyes like every fence in America had personally insulted her.

Before that, she was all glassware and weather apps, all soft sweaters, all *don’t start*, all “you make everything into a war.” Then Churchill Downs happened. The hats, the mint juleps, the velvet ropes, the millionaires smiling with teeth like stable doors, the horses sweating under garlands while men in linen explained bloodlines as if love were a ledger. One colt stumbled behind the paddock—just a hitch, just a tremor, just a tiny apocalypse in one magnificent leg—and she heard it. Not the crowd. Not the trumpet. Not the old money laughing in its bourbon perfume.

She heard the animal inside the industry screaming.

After that, she stopped returning my calls and started leaving pamphlets under windshield wipers: **NO GODS, NO GELDINGS, NO KINGS**. She shaved one side of her head. She wore a thrifted riding jacket with the crest torn off. She said thoroughbreds were the aristocracy’s prisoners, bred like dynasties, broken like tenants, raced like debts. She said the rich had invented beauty as a cover story for extraction. She said every racetrack was a cathedral built on ankles.

And me? I was still standing in our ruined kitchen, holding the mug she never took, reheating coffee like a widower in training. I wanted to talk about us. She wanted to talk about feedlots, stud fees, the economics of spectacle, the way suffering gets braided into tradition until it looks like heritage. I said, “You left me.” She said, “You’re using possessive language.” I said, “I loved you.” She said, “Love is not a stall.”

Then she joined them—the Thoroughbred Liberation Front, which may or may not have had five members and a group chat named after a dead mare. They met in basements beneath vegan bakeries. They argued about sabotage and symbolism, about whether velvet ropes counted as instruments of oppression, about whether a horse knew it was property or only knew the bit, the whip, the gate, the panic of thunderous bodies running because everything behind them was louder than God.

I saw her once after that, at a protest outside an auction house, rain flattening her hair to her skull, shouting at men who bought living creatures with inherited money and called it sport. She looked holy. She looked deranged. She looked like the woman who once cried during a toothpaste commercial because the golden retriever got old. I wanted to take her hand, but her hands were full of rage and soaked cardboard.

“Do you miss me?” I asked.

She laughed like a gate springing open.

Behind her, the crowd chanted for the horses, for the workers mucking stalls at dawn, for the broken-backed grooms and the boys paid under the table, for the mares bred until their bodies became factories, for every animal dressed in silk so men could gamble on its fear. The police lined up in plastic armor, servants of order, guarding the doors where the wealthy entered beneath umbrellas carried by other people.

Class war smells like wet pavement, cheap coffee, and expensive leather.

Romantic ruin smells almost the same.

I tried to tell her I had changed, though I had not. I tried to say I understood, though I only understood the shape of losing. She had found a grief larger than me and married it in public. She had traded our bed for a movement, our future for a slogan, my name for the names of horses I could not pronounce, each one a hymn and an indictment: Damascus, Ruffian, Eight Belles, Barbaro—saints of the snapped tendon, martyrs of the finish line.

And maybe that is what destroyed us: not another lover, not boredom, not the usual slow mildew of two people failing to become one life. It was Kentucky. It was the grandstand. It was the spectacle of beautiful bodies being spent for applause. It was the sudden knowledge that cruelty can wear a ribbon. It was her realizing the world was a locked barn and I was asking if we could please just talk about my feelings.

Now she sends postcards with no return address. A horse in a field. A burning trophy. A quote from some anarchist veterinarian. Once, just one sentence:

**I hope someday you love something enough to betray your own comfort.**

I keep it on the fridge beside a photo of us from before, when she still believed in brunch, when I still believed romance could remain private, when the horses were only horses in the distance, running in circles for people who never learned the names of the things they destroyed.

At night I dream of hooves on marble.

I dream she is opening every gate in Kentucky.

I dream the thoroughbreds pour through the mansions like weather, like judgment, like music made of muscle and terror, while the rich climb their staircases clutching silver and deeds, and my ex stands in the foyer, wild-eyed, laughing, covered in mud, more beautiful than forgiveness.

And I am there too, somehow, useless as ever, holding out my hands.

Not to stop her.

Not anymore.

Just to see if anything living will run toward me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph poem with compressed words and strange enjambment about the Kentucky Derby turning apocalyptic, all the horses dying, cannibals and thieves, Bentleys crashing, and lovers carrying each other through NYC.
counterfactuals.output: At the KentuckyDerby the sky unstitched its brass hymn and the horses, all thunderknees and silk-lunged terror, fell / one by one into the red grammar of the track, while cannibals in churchhats blessed the smoke with their teeth and thieves pocketed the names of the dead; Bentleys, black as guilty prayers, crashed through mintjulep glass and velvet ropes, their chrome mouths shrieking hosanna / hosanna / none spared; and far away, or after, or inside the same apocalypse, lovers in NYC carried each other over subway rivers, past bodegas burning like small suns, shoulder to shoulder, wound to wound, whispering keepbreathing keepbreathing as ash snowed down on Fifth, on Queens, on every bright ruin still trying to be a city.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a surreal anti-horse-racing poem that sounds like a fever dream: mint juleps, white gloves, Grade 1 stakes, broken-legged horses, Japanese slaughterhouses, blue ribbons, millionaires, and a repeated phrase like “how very are we.”
counterfactuals.output:
**How Very Are We**

At the track the mint juleps sweat green moons,  
white gloves applaud like moths in a chapel,  
and the trumpet opens its golden mouth  
to pour bees into the ears of millionaires.

How very are we, how very are we.

Grade 1 stakes gleam like knives in a velvet cake,  
blue ribbons bloom from the necks of nightmares,  
and every hat in the grandstand is a little white cloud  
refusing to rain.

The horses run with cathedral lungs,  
with thunder stitched into their ankles,  
with names like *Silk Empire* and *Mercy’s Debt*,  
while men with binoculars count God in fractions.

How very are we, how very are we.

A leg becomes a question no one wants answered.  
A screen rises—blue as a ribbon, blue as denial—  
and behind it the grass learns a new red alphabet.  
The crowd sips mint and pretends the sky is normal.

Somewhere, a van waits with its mouth open.  
Somewhere after the roses, after the cameras,  
after the millionaire’s grin polished bright as a spoon,  
a horse is translated into numbers,  
then silence,  
then freight.

How very are we, how very are we.

In the fever-night I see Japanese slaughterhouses  
lit like vending machines at the edge of a dream,  
steel doors breathing, fluorescent angels humming,  
the ghosts of champions standing in line  
with blue ribbons tied around their broken legs.

They ask the white gloves to clap softer.  
They ask the juleps to stop smelling like gardens.  
They ask the grandstand to unbuild itself, board by board,  
until only a field remains—  
wet, dark, forgiving.

But the millionaires are eating applause.  
The bettors are praying to tiny torn tickets.  
The announcer’s voice gallops on without a body:  
and down the stretch they come, and down, and down,  
and down into the sugar bowl,  
into the trophy case,  
into the lovely American mouth.

How very are we, how very are we.

O beautiful animal with the engine heart,  
forgive our roses, our odds, our polished shoes.  
Forgive the cameras that loved you only while flying.  
Forgive the blue ribbon for pretending  
it was not a leash.

At dawn the track is empty,  
except for hoofprints filling with mint,  
except for a pair of white gloves crawling away,  
except for the fever whispering from the rail:

How very are we.  
How very are we.  
How very.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
